findings.title: Stale denial cache can block legitimate access for up to 30s after a permission grant
findings.body: The newly introduced permDenialCache is consulted at the very start of Service.Check (lines 116-121) and short-circuits to Allowed=false before the permCache or the database are touched. There is no invalidation tied to permission changes (grants, role/team membership changes, deletions). Once any (namespace, userUID, action, name, parent) tuple has produced a deny response, that deny is cached for shortCacheTTL (30s) and will be returned for every subsequent request, even if the underlying database now grants the permission. This is a regression introduced by the PR and works against its stated goal of letting users access newly created resources: any prior deny that happened to land in the cache for the same (name, parent) tuple will hold the new permission back for up to 30s. Consider invalidating the denial entry whenever a permission grant or revocation affects the cached tuple, or use a much shorter TTL so the cache behaves as a brief burst guard rather than a 30s negative answer.

findings.title: Test does not actually verify that denial cache overrides a permissive permCache
findings.body: In TestService_CacheCheck / 'Should deny on explicit cache deny entry', the permCache is seeded with map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false} and the comment says 'Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked'. With the value false, checkPermission already returns false for that scope, so the subtest passes whether or not the permCache is consulted and does not demonstrate the precedence it claims. To actually verify that the denial cache overrides an otherwise-permissive permCache, the seeded value should be true (e.g. map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": true}).

findings.title: No test covers a stale denial cache blocking access after a permission grant
findings.body: The denial cache can hold a deny entry for up to 30s after a user was last denied for a (name, parent, action) tuple. There is no test that asserts (and therefore no guard against) the regression scenario: a prior deny is cached for the user, but the underlying store now grants the permission, and Service.Check still returns Allowed=false because the denial cache short-circuits before the new fallback-to-DB path. Adding such a test would either confirm the 30s window is acceptable, or catch it if invalidation is later added.
